COAL THEFT

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We uncover a coal theft scam that in part contributes to South Africans are being plunged into darkness as loadshedding makes a comeback in 2019.

Unique Selling Point:
- CRIME TREND IMPACTING ON SOUTH AFRICANS
- CONFRONT
- FOOTAGE OF DROP OFF

Summary:
Opportunistic criminals target transport company drivers to steal loads and loads of coal for a small fee – while the owners meant to receive the coal are unaware and run huge losses that they can’t account for.

We expose the intricate scam and confront one of the buyers of the stolen coal.

Further information:
HOW THE SCAM WORKS
1. Transporters will be contracted to move tons of coal from a mine (POINT A) to a processing plant or power station or railway station for export (POINT B).
2. Collection slips are issued when the trucks are loaded at POINT A.
3. At POINT B –delivery notes are issued when the loads are dropped off.
4. BUT not all the loads make it from POINT A to POINT B.
5. Drivers are approached by a middleman to drop the load off at another location along the route between A & B for a fee of R2500 – R3000 cash.
6. Delivery notes are jippo-ed and the receiving company at POINT B is none the wiser of the loss.

HOW BIG IS THE PROBLEM?
This is not an isolated problem – coal theft plagues the industry across South Africa. The black market for coal is thriving because there is a huge demand for coal locally and for export. So if you can get a cheap load that you can sell at premium prices – dodgy dealers are willing to look the other way.

LET’s TALK MONEY
An average load is worth between R18 000 and R25 000 – the driver gets paid R2500 – R3000, the middleman will take his cut, the insiders supplying the dodgy delivery notes will get a cut and then buyer will get a full load a discounted price because the origin is questionable.

LOSSES
The stolen loads would have been paid for the company meant to receive the cargo because the paperwork in terms of the jippo-ed delivery notes will check out. But the dodgy dealers buying the stolen loads will then re-sell the cargo back into the market – essentially one loads would be paid for TWICE!

Because there are insiders involved, the paperwork checks out – but it is only when stock takes are done by the receiving companies that the losses are noted. For example, a company would have paid for 100 000 tones, but only received 80 000.

HOW DO WE KNOW IT’S HAPPENING?
TECHNOLOGY!
Some transporters have installed sophisticated tracking systems that not only monitor the trucks movements, but also when exactly the cargo is off loaded. When the tipping mechanism on the truck is engaged a video camera is activated recording the physically delivery along with the GPS co-ordinates of the drop off.

OUR CASE STUDY
RS Regal Transporters noted that their drivers were making unauthorized stops – they did an internal investigation and uncovered that they were stealing loads. They then called in private investigator, Danie Day to take the investigation further. He managed to link some of the drivers to thefts in May and June going through back logged tracker reports. But in August they caught them red handed.

The coal was loaded at a mine, destined to be dropped off at train station for transportation to Richardsbay for export. But it got offloaded at near by site. Here the stolen A-grade coal will be mixed with a low grade coal and then sold to power stations and industry using coal fired machines.

THE BUYER IN OUR CASE STUDY
Jaco Venter rents the yard and admits to having bought loads from the middleman – but denies knowing it was stolen. He has not been arrested – nor has he been given a warning statement while the police are meant to conduct there investigation. He should have been charged with possession of stolen goods.

HOW DO WE TELL THE STORY?
- We follow the trial of the investigation, the discoveries
- We’ll do re-enactments of the middleman approaching the drivers….money changing hands
- We include the technology showing how solid the evidence is against the drivers
- Footage of the tipping of the stolen coal
- Creative Maps showing the movement of the trucks and deviations.
- We then confront the buyer

INDUSTRY EXPERT – POERIE VAN ROOYEN
Poerie van Rooyen heads up the coal theft investigations for a group of mines and has been working in this particular field for the last decade. He will explain the black market and how the coal gets traded – that it is a national issue, that often power stations end up paying twice for the same load and in some cases end up receiving substandard loads that impact on the running of power stations and contribute to breakdowns.

CONFRONT – CHASING THE LEADS
We go looking for Jaco Venter and go confront him. If we manage to get the details of the “broker / middleman” we’ll chase those leads as well.


INTERVIEWS
- TRANSPORTER - RS REGAL
- DRIVER - HIDDEN ID - EXPLAIN HOW THEY GET APPROACHED AND HOW MUCH THEY GET PAID
- PRIVATE INVESTIGATOR - DANIE DAY - HOW THEY CAUGHT THE DRIVER
- INDUSTRY EXPERT - POERIE VAN ROOYEN - BIGGER PICTURE, CRIME TRENDS
- CONFRONT - JACO VENTER

Press Release:


Coal Theft
It used to be that some commodities just weren’t worth stealing but the theft of coal has now become highly organised and lucrative. Opportunistic criminals in Mpumalanga move in on transport company drivers to help them steal the coal – while the unsuspecting owners meant to receive the coal are unaware and run huge losses that they can’t account for. Some coal-fired power stations possibly pay twice for the coal they need to keep going – and it’s part of the reason why electricity costs keep soaring. Carte Blanche investigates.
Producer: Nicky Troll
Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli


Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: Despite its dirty reputation, coal is in high demand across local and global markets competing for the commodity.

LINK: With Eskom trying to avoid loadshedding and an international export market paying top dollar – the black market for coal is taking off with criminals trading thousands of tons of stolen coal – load by load.

DANIE: This is like economical sabotage – they are stealing //CUT// not millions, but it gets up to billions INT3 M4

VO: Coal gets transported along South African roads every day from mines, to either power stations, siding yards for export, or furnaces used by local industry.

Syndicates offer drivers cash to divert their loads to alternate locations – essentially stealing the cargo from its intended delivery destination.

DRIVER: They give you R3000 – sometimes 2.5 //INT2 M1/

VO: Truck driver, Thabo, was recently caught out stealing loads of coal – he says he was approached by an organiser, or a middleman, when he stopped to get food.

DRIVER: // they come with the big money – like R180 – you see it in the car
MAC: How do you know where to go to offload?
DRIVER: They will tell you – but it’s not too far CUT INT2 M3 // // they come and said 2 km different to where you are delivering./ CUT / INT3 M1 There at Bethal they’ve got a place, there at Witbank they’ve got a place, there at Bronkhorstspruit there is, // there are many INT3 M2

VO: It’s pretty simple:
- The truck will depart with a load of coal purchased from Point A destined for a company at Point B,
- But the coal doesn’t get to Point B – instead, it’s offloaded at an illegal coal yard nearby at POINT C.
- An Insider at Point B supplies fraudulent weighbridge slips, making it look like the load was received.
- The transporter will still get paid, because according to the system, everything is in order.

LINK: It’s a lucrative scam – the drivers make hard cash in hand – no overheads, no feul, no tyres, no maintenance - using his employer’s truck, he sells a load of coal to a third party – pockets the money.

RENIER: they go behind your back and steal from your customers. INT1 M4 // one of the drivers // said he earned a R157000 a month. INT1 M12

VO: Transporter Renier Erasmus realises if his drivers are caught, there could be serious implications for his company, RS Regal - even if he was not involved.

RENIER: Say the mine came to me first and tell me – ok, we catch your guys stealing coal then I must pay the coal and I can loose my contract and if you are branded that you are stealing coal – who is going to give you work? INT1 M11

VO: When he picked up irregularities last year, he called on private investigator Danie Day. The investigation revealed that some RS Regal drivers were definitely involved with coal theft.

DANIE: This is the PTO movement report which is fitted to trailer – so when they tip it you can see the position // INT5 M2 Date and time you can see, this is the original document where they load, this is where they are meant to offload – the siding // INT5 M1//// but this does not correspond – with the actual tracking or the tipping of the fleet management = this proves that our truck and trailer was not offloading at this particular premises at this date and time. INT6 M1

VO: Coal theft is not an isolated crime trend, it has infiltrated the entire industry - investigators have identified around 30 illegal coal yards operating in Mpumalanga.

There is range of rules and regulations that apply to operators in the coal industry, explains Mining Sector Investigator, Poerie van Rooyen.

POERIE: // A lot of the small blending yards are not following the rules. If one looks at the receivers that we find with the blending yards, //, 99% of them did not apply and are not following the rules and regulations. INT3 M1

LINK: Depending on the grade of the coal a 30 ton load can fetch anything from R18 000 to 45 000 – on the black market it will go for half that – pushing the profit for the criminals way up.

VO: They sell it back as legitimate products – often, to the same consumers the loads have been stolen from.

POERIE: I do believe that the receivers at the end of the day do have their market whether it’s for export or whether it’s for the power stations, // or whether it’s for // industrial areas that are using coal // INT1 M18

VO: So why should you care as a consumer?

In this scenario, the same load is essentially being paid for twice – once when they think it’s been received, and then again when they unwittingly buy the stolen load.

Contributing to the price of electricity and adding to the country’s power struggles.

DANIE: Let’s say a specific mine is supposed to deliver an amount to a power station – there’s say 800 000 tons // by the 24th of the month they realise but we’ve order 800 000 but we only received 600 000 because we cant keep the electricity on // the book keeping looks good – but when they do stock taking the loads not there. INT3 M5

VO: This criminality forces transporters like Erasmus to spend money on increased security measures.

MAC: It can’t be cheap?
RENIER: R25 000 per truck
MAC: cuts into profits
RENIER: it is frustrating but to keep our work we must do it – and it’s, it’s frustrating because the authorities does nothing about this. INT1 M17

VO: That’s exactly what happened in the case Danie investigated in August - when he tracked and traced two loads of stolen coal, that RS Regal drivers delivered to a yard, just 1.9km from their actual destination.

MAC: Have you been able to identify who’s buying the stolen coal?
DANIE: the guy that we identified there is a person by the name of Jaco // INT1 M14

VO: We decided to visit the yard that Jaco rented last year in Black Hill, Witbank.

UPSOUND: looking for Jaco Venter?

VO: Apparently there is a new tenant - John Moganedi worked as a guard when Venter operated from these premises.

JOHN: // when they discovered the stolen coal – we started to know there was something fishy and his business was not operating well.

VO: But shortly after the police visit and the confiscation of the stolen coal, John says Venter stopped operating from this yard.

MAC: Where is jaco now?
JOHN: Jaco is around all over Middleburg and Witbank… INT1 M7 // the rumours are saying they saw him around and he is still operating. CUT END

VO: When the stolen RS Regal loads were recovered, Jaco Venter said in the presence of police and investigators, that he bought the coal from a so-called broker and had no knowledge of the loads origin and intended destination.

DANIE:// His attitude was I don’t care who I buy form whether it is stolen or not – I buy from the broker and then obliviously I sell it again. INT1 M15

VO: But that’s not what Venter’s affadavit says according to Police Spokesperson Brigadier Leonard Hlati.

BRIG HLATI: he came and found that coal in his yard and he said he did not give anyone permission to offload that coal yard. INT2 M3
MAC: He could be lying //
BRIG HLATI: I don’t want to respond to that question I just want to maintain what he disclosed in his affidavit to us. In other issuesis involved or not must be left to us. INT1 M17
MAC: your members and what they are doing is not adding up.. INT2 M2
BRIG HLATI: // the dockets were just in front of me, I saw them and they have explained to me and in terms of the investigation we are happy INT2 M7

VO: No action has been taken against Venter.

LINK: JV no longer operating from here, as you heard from the guys, but they they have given us the number….

VO: // We tracked Venter down to his new yard in Middleburg.

UPSOUND: Jaco, Mac from CB….

M: RS found coal on your land // where was that coal coming from? Where did you get that coal.
J: to be honest I don’t know about those loads
M: what do you mean you don’t know
J: this is the only yard I have
M: before you were here we have evidence to show you were operating somewhere else – RS regal found you with two loads of coal that people had bribed drivers to drop off – and you in front of police, in front of police said you got it from a broker.
J: That’s where I’m getting it from - a broker // INT1 M17
M: either you or your broker are the thief – one of the two
J: do you think the broker going to tell me this is the turck I’m using, it’s stolen, it’s hijacked – it’s stolen coal? // INT1 M32
M: how much are you buying it for?
J: 10 cent
M: 10 cents for what?
J: per truck//
M: You getting a truck load for 10 cents
J: my prices and off take agreements are confidential – so you know what, to be honest with you – it has nothing to do you with you, not with you, not with you, not with any Tom, Dick or Harry – it has nothing to do with no one. INT1 M25
M: you don’t care where it comes from
J: not my problem where it comes from
M: that means you don’t care if it stolen
J: I don’t know if it stolen. // how do I know it’s stolen INT1 M9 //
M: are you innocent?
J: yes I am
M: tell us who the broker is because that the person selling stolen coal
J: Why must I give up my broker? INT1 M33

VO: Later he sent us a number for his broker, Prosper – a self proclaimed “Supreme Hustler” – he also claimed ignorance.

MAC: He said you are his broker – he got the coal from you?
PROSPER CALL…Yah, but I don’t know RS Regal

VO: The police apparently couldn’t even reach Prosper to investigate any links – so the only arrests were the RS Regal drivers.

But industry role players feel the syndicates are not being pursued criminally.

POERIE: The biggest concern for us is that the small fish are getting caught, and the organisers and the receivers and the end-receiver at the end of the day is not getting arrested. INT1 M7 // as soon the organisers can be addressed and the receivers can be addressed – the market will stop. INT2 M11

VO: Brigadier Hlati insists it’s not that simple, investigations have to take their course.

BRIG HLATI: our investigation is open we are not only focused on the drivers, // CUTINT3 M33// there are some things I am not at liberty to divulge here because they are under investigated – some of your questions are too operational in nature that I can not open up to tell things we are doing as police and we need to mindful of that and allow the processes to unfold without being hindered. INT2 M7

VO: But in the meantime, transporters like Eramus will continue to be bear the brunt.

RENIER: the authorities must help us catching // CUT the guy on the end who is buying the coal, we can fire all our drivers and replace them on a daily basis, but if you don’t catch the buyer, then tomorrow they can steal again. INT1 M20


 
PROMOS

PROMO 1

PROMO 2
VO: Coal theft syndicates offer truck drivers cash to divert their loads – essentially stealing the cargo from its intended delivery destination – costing consumers.

DANIE: This is like economical sabotage – they are stealing //CUT// not millions, but it gets up to billions INT3 M4

PROMO 3
VO: Coal theft syndicates use truck drivers to steal thousands of tons of coal, trading it on the black market through a network of organisers and receivers.

POERIE: The sooner the organisers can be addressed and the receivers can be addressed – the market will stop.


PROMO 4

DANIE: This is like economical sabotage – they are stealing //CUT// not millions, but it gets up to billions INT3 M4

VO: The stolen coal gets traded on the black market through a network of organisers and receivers

DRIVER: They give you R3000 – sometimes 2.5 //INT2 M1/ VO: Truck driver, Thabo, was recently caught out stealing loads of coal – he says he was approached by an organiser, or a middleman, when he stopped to get food. DRIVER: // they come with the big money – like R180 – you see it in the car MAC: How do you know where to go to offload? DRIVER: They will tell you – but it’s not too far CUT INT2 M3 // // they come and said 2 km different to where you are delivering./ CUT / INT3 M1 There at Bethal they’ve got a place, there at Witbank they’ve got a place, there at Bronkhorstspruit there is, // there are many INT3 M2 VO: It’s pretty simple: - The truck will depart with a load of coal purchased from Point A destined for a company at Point B, - But the coal doesn’t get to Point B – instead, it’s offloaded at an illegal coal yard nearby at POINT C. - An Insider at Point B supplies fraudulent weighbridge slips, making it look like the load was received. - The transporter will still get paid, because according to the system, everything is in order. LINK: It’s a lucrative scam – the drivers make hard cash in hand – no overheads, no feul, no tyres, no maintenance - using his employer’s truck, he sells a load of coal to a third party – pockets the money. RENIER: they go behind your back and steal from your customers. INT1 M4 // one of the drivers // said he earned a R157000 a month. INT1 M12 VO: Transporter Renier Erasmus realises if his drivers are caught, there could be serious implications for his company, RS Regal - even if he was not involved. RENIER: Say the mine came to me first and tell me – ok, we catch your guys stealing coal then I must pay the coal and I can loose my contract and if you are branded that you are stealing coal – who is going to give you work? INT1 M11 VO: When he picked up irregularities last year, he called on private investigator Danie Day. The investigation revealed that some RS Regal drivers were definitely involved with coal theft. DANIE: This is the PTO movement report which is fitted to trailer – so when they tip it you can see the position // INT5 M2 Date and time you can see, this is the original document where they load, this is where they are meant to offload – the siding // INT5 M1//// but this does not correspond – with the actual tracking or the tipping of the fleet management = this proves that our truck and trailer was not offloading at this particular premises at this date and time. INT6 M1 VO: Coal theft is not an isolated crime trend, it has infiltrated the entire industry - investigators have identified around 30 illegal coal yards operating in Mpumalanga. There is range of rules and regulations that apply to operators in the coal industry, explains Mining Sector Investigator, Poerie van Rooyen. POERIE: // A lot of the small blending yards are not following the rules. If one looks at the receivers that we find with the blending yards, //, 99% of them did not apply and are not following the rules and regulations. INT3 M1 LINK: Depending on the grade of the coal a 30 ton load can fetch anything from R18 000 to 45 000 – on the black market it will go for half that – pushing the profit for the criminals way up. VO: They sell it back as legitimate products – often, to the same consumers the loads have been stolen from. POERIE: I do believe that the receivers at the end of the day do have their market whether it’s for export or whether it’s for the power stations, // or whether it’s for // industrial areas that are using coal // INT1 M18 VO: So why should you care as a consumer? In this scenario, the same load is essentially being paid for twice – once when they think it’s been received, and then again when they unwittingly buy the stolen load. Contributing to the price of electricity and adding to the country’s power struggles. DANIE: Let’s say a specific mine is supposed to deliver an amount to a power station – there’s say 800 000 tons // by the 24th of the month they realise but we’ve order 800 000 but we only received 600 000 because we cant keep the electricity on // the book keeping looks good – but when they do stock taking the loads not there. INT3 M5 VO: This criminality forces transporters like Erasmus to spend money on increased security measures. MAC: It can’t be cheap? RENIER: R25 000 per truck MAC: cuts into profits RENIER: it is frustrating but to keep our work we must do it – and it’s, it’s frustrating because the authorities does nothing about this. INT1 M17 VO: That’s exactly what happened in the case Danie investigated in August - when he tracked and traced two loads of stolen coal, that RS Regal drivers delivered to a yard, just 1.9km from their actual destination. MAC: Have you been able to identify who’s buying the stolen coal? DANIE: the guy that we identified there is a person by the name of Jaco // INT1 M14 VO: We decided to visit the yard that Jaco rented last year in Black Hill, Witbank. UPSOUND: looking for Jaco Venter? VO: Apparently there is a new tenant - John Moganedi worked as a guard when Venter operated from these premises. JOHN: // when they discovered the stolen coal – we started to know there was something fishy and his business was not operating well. VO: But shortly after the police visit and the confiscation of the stolen coal, John says Venter stopped operating from this yard. MAC: Where is jaco now? JOHN: Jaco is around all over Middleburg and Witbank… INT1 M7 // the rumours are saying they saw him around and he is still operating. CUT END VO: When the stolen RS Regal loads were recovered, Jaco Venter said in the presence of police and investigators, that he bought the coal from a so-called broker and had no knowledge of the loads origin and intended destination. DANIE:// His attitude was I don’t care who I buy form whether it is stolen or not – I buy from the broker and then obliviously I sell it again. INT1 M15 VO: But that’s not what Venter’s affadavit says according to Police Spokesperson Brigadier Leonard Hlati. BRIG HLATI: he came and found that coal in his yard and he said he did not give anyone permission to offload that coal yard. INT2 M3 MAC: He could be lying // BRIG HLATI: I don’t want to respond to that question I just want to maintain what he disclosed in his affidavit to us. In other issuesis involved or not must be left to us. INT1 M17 MAC: your members and what they are doing is not adding up.. INT2 M2 BRIG HLATI: // the dockets were just in front of me, I saw them and they have explained to me and in terms of the investigation we are happy INT2 M7 VO: No action has been taken against Venter. LINK: JV no longer operating from here, as you heard from the guys, but they they have given us the number…. VO: // We tracked Venter down to his new yard in Middleburg. UPSOUND: Jaco, Mac from CB…. M: RS found coal on your land // where was that coal coming from? Where did you get that coal. J: to be honest I don’t know about those loads M: what do you mean you don’t know J: this is the only yard I have M: before you were here we have evidence to show you were operating somewhere else – RS regal found you with two loads of coal that people had bribed drivers to drop off – and you in front of police, in front of police said you got it from a broker. J: That’s where I’m getting it from - a broker // INT1 M17 M: either you or your broker are the thief – one of the two J: do you think the broker going to tell me this is the turck I’m using, it’s stolen, it’s hijacked – it’s stolen coal? // INT1 M32 M: how much are you buying it for? J: 10 cent M: 10 cents for what? J: per truck// M: You getting a truck load for 10 cents J: my prices and off take agreements are confidential – so you know what, to be honest with you – it has nothing to do you with you, not with you, not with you, not with any Tom, Dick or Harry – it has nothing to do with no one. INT1 M25 M: you don’t care where it comes from J: not my problem where it comes from M: that means you don’t care if it stolen J: I don’t know if it stolen. // how do I know it’s stolen INT1 M9 // M: are you innocent? J: yes I am M: tell us who the broker is because that the person selling stolen coal J: Why must I give up my broker? INT1 M33 VO: Later he sent us a number for his broker, Prosper – a self proclaimed “Supreme Hustler” – he also claimed ignorance. MAC: He said you are his broker – he got the coal from you? PROSPER CALL…Yah, but I don’t know RS Regal VO: The police apparently couldn’t even reach Prosper to investigate any links – so the only arrests were the RS Regal drivers. But industry role players feel the syndicates are not being pursued criminally. POERIE: The biggest concern for us is that the small fish are getting caught, and the organisers and the receivers and the end-receiver at the end of the day is not getting arrested. INT1 M7 // as soon the organisers can be addressed and the receivers can be addressed – the market will stop. INT2 M11 VO: Brigadier Hlati insists it’s not that simple, investigations have to take their course. BRIG HLATI: our investigation is open we are not only focused on the drivers, // CUTINT3 M33// there are some things I am not at liberty to divulge here because they are under investigated – some of your questions are too operational in nature that I can not open up to tell things we are doing as police and we need to mindful of that and allow the processes to unfold without being hindered. INT2 M7 VO: But in the meantime, transporters like Eramus will continue to be bear the brunt. RENIER: the authorities must help us catching // CUT the guy on the end who is buying the coal, we can fire all our drivers and replace them on a daily basis, but if you don’t catch the buyer, then tomorrow they can steal again. INT1 M20 PROMOS PROMO 1 VO: Thousands of tons of coal get traded on the black market across South Africa – often costing you the consumer and adding to our loadshedding woes. Carte Blanche investigates. PROMO 2 VO: Coal theft syndicates offer truck drivers cash to divert their loads – essentially stealing the cargo from its intended delivery destination – costing consumers. DANIE: This is like economical sabotage – they are stealing //CUT// not millions, but it gets up to billions INT3 M4 PROMO 3 VO: Coal theft syndicates use truck drivers to steal thousands of tons of coal, trading it on the black market through a network of organisers and receivers. POERIE: The sooner the organisers can be addressed and the receivers can be addressed – the market will stop. PROMO 4 VO: We uncover a coal theft scam where thousands of tons of coal gets traded on the black market across South Africa - often costing you the consumer and adding to our loadshedding woes. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We uncover a coal theft scam that in part contributes to South Africans are being plunged into darkness as loadshedding makes a comeback in 2019.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: - CRIME TREND IMPACTING ON SOUTH AFRICANS - CONFRONT - FOOTAGE OF DROP OFF
metadata.Summary: Opportunistic criminals target transport company drivers to steal loads and loads of coal for a small fee – while the owners meant to receive the coal are unaware and run huge losses that they can’t account for. We expose the intricate scam and confront one of the buyers of the stolen coal.
metadata.Further information: HOW THE SCAM WORKS 1. Transporters will be contracted to move tons of coal from a mine (POINT A) to a processing plant or power station or railway station for export (POINT B). 2. Collection slips are issued when the trucks are loaded at POINT A. 3. At POINT B –delivery notes are issued when the loads are dropped off. 4. BUT not all the loads make it from POINT A to POINT B. 5. Drivers are approached by a middleman to drop the load off at another location along the route between A & B for a fee of R2500 – R3000 cash. 6. Delivery notes are jippo-ed and the receiving company at POINT B is none the wiser of the loss. HOW BIG IS THE PROBLEM? This is not an isolated problem – coal theft plagues the industry across South Africa. The black market for coal is thriving because there is a huge demand for coal locally and for export. So if you can get a cheap load that you can sell at premium prices – dodgy dealers are willing to look the other way. LET’s TALK MONEY An average load is worth between R18 000 and R25 000 – the driver gets paid R2500 – R3000, the middleman will take his cut, the insiders supplying the dodgy delivery notes will get a cut and then buyer will get a full load a discounted price because the origin is questionable. LOSSES The stolen loads would have been paid for the company meant to receive the cargo because the paperwork in terms of the jippo-ed delivery notes will check out. But the dodgy dealers buying the stolen loads will then re-sell the cargo back into the market – essentially one loads would be paid for TWICE! Because there are insiders involved, the paperwork checks out – but it is only when stock takes are done by the receiving companies that the losses are noted. For example, a company would have paid for 100 000 tones, but only received 80 000. HOW DO WE KNOW IT’S HAPPENING? TECHNOLOGY! Some transporters have installed sophisticated tracking systems that not only monitor the trucks movements, but also when exactly the cargo is off loaded. When the tipping mechanism on the truck is engaged a video camera is activated recording the physically delivery along with the GPS co-ordinates of the drop off. OUR CASE STUDY RS Regal Transporters noted that their drivers were making unauthorized stops – they did an internal investigation and uncovered that they were stealing loads. They then called in private investigator, Danie Day to take the investigation further. He managed to link some of the drivers to thefts in May and June going through back logged tracker reports. But in August they caught them red handed. The coal was loaded at a mine, destined to be dropped off at train station for transportation to Richardsbay for export. But it got offloaded at near by site. Here the stolen A-grade coal will be mixed with a low grade coal and then sold to power stations and industry using coal fired machines. THE BUYER IN OUR CASE STUDY Jaco Venter rents the yard and admits to having bought loads from the middleman – but denies knowing it was stolen. He has not been arrested – nor has he been given a warning statement while the police are meant to conduct there investigation. He should have been charged with possession of stolen goods. HOW DO WE TELL THE STORY? - We follow the trial of the investigation, the discoveries - We’ll do re-enactments of the middleman approaching the drivers….money changing hands - We include the technology showing how solid the evidence is against the drivers - Footage of the tipping of the stolen coal - Creative Maps showing the movement of the trucks and deviations. - We then confront the buyer INDUSTRY EXPERT – POERIE VAN ROOYEN Poerie van Rooyen heads up the coal theft investigations for a group of mines and has been working in this particular field for the last decade. He will explain the black market and how the coal gets traded – that it is a national issue, that often power stations end up paying twice for the same load and in some cases end up receiving substandard loads that impact on the running of power stations and contribute to breakdowns. CONFRONT – CHASING THE LEADS We go looking for Jaco Venter and go confront him. If we manage to get the details of the “broker / middleman” we’ll chase those leads as well. INTERVIEWS - TRANSPORTER - RS REGAL - DRIVER - HIDDEN ID - EXPLAIN HOW THEY GET APPROACHED AND HOW MUCH THEY GET PAID - PRIVATE INVESTIGATOR - DANIE DAY - HOW THEY CAUGHT THE DRIVER - INDUSTRY EXPERT - POERIE VAN ROOYEN - BIGGER PICTURE, CRIME TRENDS - CONFRONT - JACO VENTER
